title: Adaptive batching config swap caused tail-latency cascade; request for safe unwind and verification
body:
Adaptive batching config swap caused tail-latency cascade; request for safe unwind and verification

Issue summary: Customer observed increased 95th/99th token latency and sporadic streaming disconnects immediately after we enabled an adaptive batching experiment for their tenant (coalesce_small_reqs=true, adaptive_grouping=aggressive) and a matched experimental quant profile (q8_dyn_prefetch). They requested guidance for a safe unwind: minimal customer disruption, no model-quality regressions, and a reproducible verification checklist.
Several production routes for BrightHealth AI show 95p latency up from ~180ms to 750-1200ms and periodic client stream resets. Traffic is on Dedicated pool assigned to the customer; estimated 12% of user-facing requests affected. Business impact: user timeouts and degraded UX for conversational flows; P1 SLA breach risk.
1) Tenant uses dedicated pool with tenant_id bhai-prod-42.
2) Apply optimizer profile: {coalesce_small_reqs: true, max_batch_wait_ms: 15, adaptive_grouping: aggressive, quant_profile: q8_dyn_prefetch}.
3) Replay synthetic production load (mix of short prompts and streaming long generations).
4) Observe that small concurrent requests are coalesced into heterogenous batches; KV cache thrash observed on serving nodes leading to tail amplification and occasional stream disconnects.
Excerpt from serving-runtime trace (us-east-1, node rwd-srv-11):
[2026-03-13T09:34:12.412Z] TRACE request-id=rcst-7b3a: batch-size 18 coalesced (heterogeneous seq lengths)
[2026-03-13T09:34:12.415Z] WARN kv-cache: evict: tenant=bhai-prod-42 key-prefetch-miss=0.86
[2026-03-13T09:34:12.419Z] ERROR stream: write error: upstream reset by peer (timeout)
[2026-03-13T09:34:12.422Z] PERF token-latency: p95=980ms p99=1.24s
Support captured a console trace and attached the tenant traffic sample in case file: rwd-trace-bhai-20260313.log
Initial hypothesis: the combination of aggressive coalescing and dynamic quant prefetching is causing cache eviction churn. Small requests are being combined with long-context streams producing heterogeneous batch padding; quant prefetch is populating ephemeral weights/kv entries that push hot KV entries out. This increases backend deserialization/rehydration costs and spikes tail latency.
Evidence: correlated spikes on kv-cache eviction metric and an increase in deserialization time in kernel selection traces. No model weights OOMs reported.
Triage steps performed: rolled traffic from 100% to 80% steady and split 20% to canary with conservative profile (coalesce_small_reqs=false, q8_static). Canary shows p95 back to normal.
Open hypothesis: async quant prefetch interacts with coalescing by prefetching per-batch quant tables for long-sequence items, causing eviction for recently-accessed short-context items. We need a safe unwind that avoids immediate mass rollbacks that could cause cold-start penalty for long-running conversations.
2026-03-13 10:02 - Support (Evelyn Carter): Received report from customer, reproduced in sandbox with replay. Noticed consistent kv-cache evictions when coalescing is enabled.
2026-03-13 11:10 - SRE (Ravi Menon): Recommended splitting traffic to canary and disabling coalesce_small_reqs for the tenant as quick mitigation. Prepared rollback checklist and snapshot plan.
2026-03-13 11:48 - Customer (BrightHealth AI, product lead - Anika Rao): Asked for minimal interruption plan; cannot take a full restart during business hours. Requests guidance for staged unwind and verification.
2026-03-13 13:05 - Support (Evelyn Carter): Confirmed canary with conservative settings shows stable latencies. Drafted verification checklist for safe unwind. Pending SRE action to apply toggles.
2026-03-14 08:23 - SRE (Ravi Menon): Executed staged unwind: (a) disabled coalesce_small_reqs at tenant level, (b) switched quant_profile to q8_static for new sessions, (c) left prefix/KV cache warmers running for existing sessions to reduce cold-start regressions. Monitoring shows p95 returning to ~210ms.
2026-03-14 09:00 - Customer (Anika Rao): Verified on their end; user-facing timeouts resolved for sampled flows. Asked for postmortem and follow-up mitigation to safely re-run experiment.
Workaround applied: staged unwind executed by SRE on 2026-03-14. Specific actions: (1) tenant-level toggle coalesce_small_reqs=false; (2) quant profile fallback to q8_static for new sessions via routing policy; (3) enabled transient traffic-split to keep 10% traffic on conservative canary for 2 hours for validation; (4) warmed KV cache using shadow replays for active conversations to avoid cold starts.
Outcome: p95 and p99 latencies returned to acceptable range; streaming disconnects stopped.
Follow-ups: (a) Engineering to instrument per-tenant KV eviction metrics more granularly and add alerting for eviction > 0.6 sustained over 5m. (b) Research to add coalesce-awareness to quant-prefetch (avoid per-batch prefetch for heterogeneous batches). (c) Support to prepare a tenant-facing runbook describing staged unwind steps.
Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4721 (prefetch throttle patch).
1) ENG: Add preflight simulator to model optimizer experiments that runs customer replay against coalesce+quant combos (owner: @ravi). 2) SRE: Add eviction-based alert and tenant-level rollback API docs (owner: @maria). 3) Support: Draft tenant runbook and coordinate maintenance window to re-run experiment conservatively (owner: @evelyn).

title: Late-afternoon throughput plateau: GPU slot fragmentation combined with autoscaler cooldown misconfiguration
body:
Late-afternoon throughput plateau: GPU slot fragmentation combined with autoscaler cooldown misconfiguration

Issue summary: Starting ~2026-03-12 14:05 UTC, BeaconHealth's dedicated pool in us-west-2 experienced a sustained p50/p99 throughput plateau for 40+ minutes despite overall cluster capacity appearing sufficient. Impact: customer observed ~30% drop in completed token throughput for batched /generate requests and increased queueing. The problem correlated with many short-lived GPU attaches and fragmented slot allocation across hosts. Initial hypothesis: a noisy background workload (ephemeral debug/training jobs from another tenant) caused frequent small allocations and KV cache churn; autoscaler cooldown and min-replicas configuration prevented quick consolidation, causing slot fragmentation and prolonged throughput plateau.
1) Reproduce workload shape: submit a steady stream of medium-length batched inference requests (~1k requests/min, avg seq_len 1024) to a dedicated pool pinned to BeaconHealth's tenant.
2) Inject many short-lived attach/attach-release operations from a separate tenant (simulate ephemeral debug jobs with ~10s lifetimes, 50-100 parallel short streams) on the same dedicated cluster.
3) Observe allocator logs and slot distribution via /debug/allocator and Grafana (batch-slot-utilization, gpu-attach-rate). Expect slot fragmentation and small-slot holding behavior.
Selected artifacts: grafana: /d/redwood/dedicated-pool-usw2?from=2026-03-12T13:30:00Z&to=2026-03-12T15:00:00Z (panels: slot-fragmentation, attach-rate, kv-cache-evictions); allocator log excerpt: '2026-03-12T14:07:21Z WARN slot_manager: small-slot-hold host=usw2-host-17 slot_count=3 fragmentation=0.78 tenant=beacon-health'; autoscaler events: 'scale_down deferred due to cooldown, target_replicas=4 current=6 last_scale_event=2026-03-12T13:58:09Z'; request traces: increased queueing at queue-service p95 ~420ms -> 1.2s.
- Observed high attach/release churn from tenant 'dev-sandbox-7' coincident with throughput drop. Slack thread #support: tldr in thread (https://slack.redwood/support/threads/CFJ9kLq2).
- KV cache eviction rate doubled during event, causing many requests to re-run warmup phases and increasing effective per-request GPU time.
- Autoscaler had a 10m cooldown and min_replicas configured to 4 for the pool. When ephemeral attaches freed fragmented slots, autoscaler didn't consolidate because cooldown prevented downsizing/upsizing quickly; this left many hosts with underfilled slots.
- Host-level metric nvlink_io_wait spiked on 5 hosts, matching small-stream I/O bursts from ephemeral jobs. PCIe saturation signs noted on hosts running both debug jobs and customer streaming workloads.
- Hypothesis validated: noisy short-stream tenant caused I/O noise and slot fragmentation; autoscaler cooldown prevented rapid rebalancing; scheduler/allocator favored fairness per-tenant which prevented preemption of tiny attaches.
Mitigations applied during incident:
1) Temporarily isolated 'dev-sandbox-7' by moving its pods to a different reserved pool (config change + drain), eliminating the noisy background attaches.
2) Reduced autoscaler cooldown to 90s for the affected dedicated pool and increased prewarm worker target from 2 -> 6 to reduce warmup penalty.
3) Adjusted allocator tuning to prefer consolidation when fragmentation>0.6 and combined small-slot holders under eviction policy to free contiguous slots.
Outcome: throughput returned to baseline within ~12 minutes of isolation; p99 queueing returned to normal levels and KV-eviction rate normalized.
- Engineering action item: autoscaler: add 'burst-mode' override that temporarily relaxes cooldown when attach-rate delta > X for replicated dedicated pools (PR opened gh-redwood/autoscaler#209).
- Ops: add a Prometheus alert (attach_rate_churn > threshold) to trigger automated tenant isolation or notify SRE.
- Product: document recommended tenant best-practices for dedicated pools (avoid ephemeral training/debug loads on shared physical hosts).
- Runbook: update dedicated-autoscale-playbook with consolidation play and prewarm knobs.
For impacted customers: suggestion to set a minimum 'isolation' tag on critical tenants to ensure physical separation from ephemeral workloads; temporary fix applied for BeaconHealth by applying isolation tag.

title: Provisioning failure: macOS image fails MDM enrollment for hybrid SSO users
body:
Provisioning failure: macOS image fails MDM enrollment for hybrid SSO users

Issue summary:
New hire laptop provisioning using the macOS 13.6 base image fails during automated MDM enrollment step for users who require hybrid SSO (Okta PIV + company SSO). Enrollment hangs on 'Waiting for user authentication' and the device never appears in Jamf inventory.

Impact:
- Blocks onboarding for 3 hires in the past 2 days.
- Manual image/enroll path works but requires ~30–45 minutes of tech time per device.
- Causes delays for engineering hires that need GPU-enabled workstations.

Environment:
- Office devices imaged at SJC imaging station (prod-us-west-office).
- macOS 13.6 base image built 2026-03-05.
- MDM: Jamf Pro 11.2.1.
- SSO: Okta with hybrid PIV flow + internal auth proxy.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Boot target Mac to NetBoot/auto-imaging via SJC imaging VLAN.
2) Apply base image 2026-03-05 and allow enrollment to trigger.
3) Observe endpoint stop at 'Waiting for user authentication' screen in Jamf enrollment log.
4) Device never registers in Jamf inventory (last seen status: pending enrollment).

Observed logs (excerpt):
- imaging-station.log: "mdm-enroll: start callback; handshake ok; waiting for oauth token"
- jamf-enroll.log: "ENROLLMENT_STATUS: pending_user_auth (timeout 600s)"
- okta-proxy.log: "incoming auth request: session created; SSO redirect issued; user never POSTed credentials"

Investigation notes so far:
- Rebuilt base image (2026-03-08) without changed drivers — same symptom.
- Manual enrollment via Jamf Pro console (generate enrollment URL and complete flow) does succeed for the same user on same hardware.
- Devices enrolled in staging imaging VLAN succeed with same image; difference seems tied to SJC office network's auth proxy flow.
- Packet capture on imaging VLAN shows outbound redirect to auth proxy but occasional TCP RST between imaging station and proxy at 10–20s into the flow.
- Hypothesis: corporate auth proxy (edge device in SJC) has an MTU/inspection rule that breaks the hybrid SSO flow during automated enrollment sequences.

Immediate workaround:
- Techs should use manual enrollment URL from Jamf Console when provisioning new hires at SJC until fix is applied (adds ~30–45m per device).

Next steps / action items:
- [Assigned] Networking to review auth proxy logs and firewall rules for imaging VLAN (Samuel).
- [Assigned] SSO/Identity to verify whether Okta sessions are being invalidated for automated flows (Riley Chen).
- [Assigned] Imaging/Endpoint team to provision a temporary imaging VLAN that bypasses the proxy for onboarding (Ava Nguyen).
- Collect full pcap and provide to Security for DPI inspection if permitted.
- Target remediation ETA: 2026-03-15 for either firewall rule change or proxy config update.

title: Request production change approval: controlled regional failover test (us-east -> eu-west) + feature-flag enablement
body:
Request production change approval: controlled regional failover test (us-east -> eu-west) + feature-flag enablement

Requesting formal production change approval for the Q1 2026 controlled regional failover game day (Hosted API + limited Dedicated validation) as part of the Regional Failover Automation Upgrade.

Change window
- Proposed window: 2026-01-15 10:00–11:00 PT (primary execution 10:15–10:35 PT)
- Regions: us-east (source) -> eu-west (target)
- Expected customer impact: minimal; brief elevated latency/5xx possible for a limited tenant allowlist if clients do not honor retry-after or streaming reconnect.

Scope of production changes
1) Feature-flag enablement (limited blast radius)
- Enable failover controller in production in "approval required" mode (no autonomous flips without on-call ack).
- Enable dry-run outputs + audit events for all production tenants (read-only) so we can validate signal ingestion + decisioning.
- Enable execution mode only for allowlisted tenants/routes (Hosted API: chat/generate; Dedicated: 1 internal test pool only).

2) Routing policy / signal evaluation
- Policy engine deterministic hierarchy enabled (ADR-042) for the allowlist.
- Capacity headroom signal integrated as a gating signal (do not failover if target region headroom < threshold).
- Anti-flap hold-down + rate limits enabled (ADR-043) to prevent oscillation.

3) Infra/networking prerequisites
- Confirm DNS TTL changes already applied per redwood-terraform/pr-1442 (no TTL change executed during the test window).
- No new firewall/VPC changes planned during the window.

Monitoring & success criteria
Primary dashboards (see failover-signal-dashboards-spec):
- Reachability: perf-canary cross-region probes (success rate, p95 latency)
- API error burn: 5xx burn rate + gateway timeouts
- Tail latency burn: p95/p99 by route/model for allowlisted tenants
- Capacity: target region GPU headroom + queue depth
- Automation: policy flip events, rollback events, hold-down timers
- Streaming: reconnect rate + disconnect errors (post pr-19821)

Success criteria (for approval purposes)
- Failover decision computed within 60s of induced impairment signal, with corroboration recorded.
- Executed flip (after approval) completes within 2 minutes end-to-end for allowlisted routes.
- Customer-visible error rate for allowlisted tenants does not exceed: 1% over 5 minutes (burst ok, but must recover quickly).
- No sustained overload in target region (headroom remains above the configured safety threshold; queue depth stabilizes).
- Rollback path verified (either automated rollback triggers correctly OR manual rollback completes within 5 minutes).

Rollback plan (must be executable by on-call)
- Immediate stop: disable failover controller execution flag (keep dry-run on).
- Revert routing policy overrides for allowlisted tenants/routes to baseline (pre-test policy snapshot).
- If target region overload observed: enforce load shedding (retry-after) and reduce allowlist / disable reroute.
- If any instability in controller: scale deployment to 0 and revert to manual routing workflow.
- Communications: post internal update to #incidents and #eng-sre; if any customer impact beyond allowlist, follow regional-failover-communication-playbook.

Approvals requested
- Change owner: Rafael Mendes (SRE), Miles Thornton (Failover architecture)
- Routing/control plane signoff: Mina Haddad / Ethan Park
- Observability readiness: Allison Grant
- Networking readiness: Victor Alvarez / Irene Choi (confirm DNS prerequisites and monitoring)

- Incident-bot will post failover event summaries (incident-bot/pr-412).
- We will annotate dashboards at each step; separate request INT-1149 tracks missing auto-annotations from the controller.

title: Edge rate-limiter token-bucket TTL eviction caused retry stampede and elevated 5xx across mixed embed/chat routes
body:
Edge rate-limiter token-bucket TTL eviction caused retry stampede and elevated 5xx across mixed embed/chat routes

Issue summary: BrightDocs reported sudden elevated 5xx rates (502/503) across both embedding and chat routes starting 2026-03-13 20:02 UTC. Impact: multiple customer requests failed with upstream 5xx; latency spiked and streaming sessions dropped. Environment: prod us-east, dedicated tenant for BrightDocs. Hypothesis: edge rate-limiter token-bucket TTL eviction caused per-tenant token bucket state to reset simultaneously, producing a retry stampede that saturated the api-gateway accept queue and upstream runtimes, leading to 5xx and some runtime crashes. This ticket tracks investigation, mitigations, and customer communication.
1) Send mixed traffic (short embed uploads plus chat streaming) at burst rate (~1200 rps) to tenant-alias belonging to BrightDocs in us-east.
2) Observe edge rate-limiter metrics: token_bucket_evictions rate spikes and per-tenant buckets show recent ttl expirations.
3) Client SDKs retried on 429 but misinterpreted response as transient, sending repeated hedged retries, amplifying load.
4) Api-gateway accept queue grows; upstream runtime threads hit prefetch locks and some runtimes restart with OOM-like symptoms.
Note: reproducing requires simulated ttl-eviction conditions and client retry heuristics; non-trivial in staging unless rate-limiter TTLs are reduced.

Support (2026-03-13 20:10) - Aisha: Customer BrightDocs reported a 10-15% error rate with 502/503 across both embeds and chat. Asked for tenant alias and recent request IDs. Provided request ids: rq_20260313_20_02_{a..f}.

Customer (BrightDocs Ops, 2026-03-13 20:30) - Jenna: Confirmed traffic pattern: SDK batch uploader retried aggressively on 429. We had a scheduled cron that did chunked embedding uploads at 20:00 UTC.
Engineer (2026-03-13 20:45) - Priya: Correlated events: TTL rotation job for edge cache completed at 20:01 UTC (https://runbook.redwood/ttl-rotation). Hypothesis: eviction wave + client retries caused accept queue starvation and two runtime restarts.
SRE (2026-03-13 21:05) - Marco: Rolled out hotfix on edge rate-limiter: stagger TTL sweeps across nodes and added jitter to eviction loop; monitoring for 30m. Applied conservative retry-quarantine at api-gateway for repeated hedged retries.
Support (2026-03-13 21:35) - Aisha: Customer confirmed error rate dropped to baseline ~0.2% after hotfix and temporary throttling. Monitoring to ensure no recurring spikes.
SRE (2026-03-14 09:10) - Marco: Postmortem draft started; root cause is combination of synchronous TTL eviction across edge nodes + aggressive client retry semantics that interpreted 429s as transient  and retried without backoff, amplifying pressure. Next steps listed below.
Edge metrics show token_bucket_evictions aligned across NTP-synchronized nodes -> likely coordinated eviction job or TTL drift.
Accept queue growth first observed on edge-3 then propagated via load balancer to other apigw instances.
Runtime watch-dog triggered restarts after accept queue pressure and long prefetch lock waits.
Client SDKs (brightdocs-sdk v2.3.1) had a retry change in 2.3.0 that retries on any non-200 including 429; lacking exponential backoff in bulk upload path.
No config changes from BrightDocs on 2026-03-13; their scheduled batch likely tipped the system when eviction occurred.
Related signal: small but sustained increase in kernel softirq for network handling on apigw hosts during the spike.
1) Applied tenant-level soft-rate-limit (200 rps) to BrightDocs at 20:26 UTC to break retry loop.
2) Hot-fixed edge rate-limiter: added node-level random jitter to TTL eviction jobs and limited per-eviction bucket deletes to 50/s.
3) Configured api-gateway to detect repeated hedged retries and send 429 with Retry-After header for same client fingerprint for 10s.
4) Restarted two affected runtimes in a controlled drain to recover prefetch locks; observed stable memory after restart.
5) Notified BrightDocs of recommended SDK upgrade (v2.3.2) which includes exponential backoff for bulk uploads.
6) Added temporary alert rule to detect global token_bucket_evictions rate > 100/s per region.
1) Engineering: implement persistent per-tenant token-bucket state (avoid synchronous full-region eviction) - owner: Priya - ETA: 2026-03-21.
2) Product/SDK: coordinate mandatory backoff in SDK for bulk embedding uploads and document best-practices for retry behavior - owner: Diego - ETA: 2026-03-18.
3) SRE: harden api-gateway retry-quarantine heuristics and add synthetic test covering TTL eviction + client retry storm - owner: Marco - ETA: 2026-03-16.
4) Postmortem: complete RCA and publish on Confluence and share with BrightDocs - owner: Marco - ETA: 2026-03-17.
5) Follow-up: schedule canary of TTL rotation job with smaller window and node-level staggering - owner: infra-team - ETA: 2026-03-15.
Mitigated (temporary throttles, jittered eviction). Permanent fix in progress: per-tenant bucket persistence and SDK backoff. Customer impact resolved; monitoring remains active.
2026-03-13 21:45 UTC - We implemented temporary throttles and a hotfix in the edge rate limiter to address elevated 5xx for BrightDocs; traffic has returned to normal. Engineering is implementing a permanent fix to avoid coordinated eviction events and working with SDK teams to improve retry behavior.
If customers see repeated 429/5xx during bulk uploads, upgrade to brightdocs-sdk v2.3.2 (or later) which toggles exponential backoff for uploads.

title: Connection churn from many short streams prevents prefetch reuse, causing slot erosion and sustained throughput degradation
body:
Connection churn from many short streams prevents prefetch reuse, causing slot erosion and sustained throughput degradation

Issue summary: Customer reports a gradual, sustained drop in dedicated pool throughput over several hours coincident with a high rate of short-lived connections from a single tenant. Impact: AcmeChat's p50 token throughput dropped ~35% and p99 latency increased from ~120ms to ~890ms on their dedicated reservations for several rolling windows. Environment: prod us-east, dedicated pool (reservation-id: res-84f3). Observed: high connection churn (>15k connects/min), unusually high prefetch requests per second, repeated KV cache warmups, frequent small eviction events and GPU-slot fragmentation. Expected: short streams should not starve longer batched work or cause repeated prefetch re-execution that fragments slots. This ticket captures triage, investigation notes, and mitigation attempts.
1) Provision a small dedicated reservation with mixed workloads: 20% steady long-batch traffic (seq len 1024) + 80% short chat streams (avg 4 tokens) from a single tenant.
2) Simulate high connection churn: open/close websocket connections at ~250 RPS per client for 60+ minutes across 100 parallel clients.
3) Observe scheduler allocation churn, repeated prefetch calls in serving-runtime, and falling p50 throughput on the dedicated pool dashboards.
4) Capture metrics from /metrics and /debug endpoints for prefetch_requests_total, evictions_total, gpu_slot_free_fraction.
5) Re-run with client-side keepalive (30s) to compare behavior — mitigation is expected if churn is root cause.
[2026-03-10T14:22:03Z] prefetch: tenant=acmechat req_id=8f7cd prefetch_start seq_id=312 ttl_ms=60000
[2026-03-10T14:22:03Z] scheduler: allocate slot gpu=gpux012 reservation=res-84f3 reason=short_stream
[2026-03-10T14:22:04Z] eviction: slot=slot-2 tenant=acmechat cause=prefetch_collision
[2026-03-10T14:22:38Z] serving-runtime: kv-cache-miss tenant=acmechat key=conv-9b1a miss_count=47
[2026-03-10T15:03:11Z] nvlink: peer-drop detected on gpux012 (kernel 0xffff) — transient IO errors, correlates with eviction spikes
p50 throughput baseline: 12k tokens/s -> degraded to 7.9k tokens/s over 2 hours
prefetch_requests_total: increased 5x from baseline during the incident window
gpu_slot_free_fraction: dropped from 0.28 -> 0.05 during sustained churn
evictions_total: saw periodic spikes aligned with connection bursts
Initial hypothesis: a dominant tenant generating a high volume of very short streams causes repeated prefetch attempts and frequent allocation/eviction cycles, which fragment GPU slots (slot erosion) and reduce effective batch sizes for other tenants. Support validated correlation between tenant X (AcmeChat) connection churn and pool-level degradation via dashboards: dedicated-reservation res-84f3. SRE captured serving-runtime traces showing prefetch_start events for conversation keys that are immediately abandoned when clients disconnect; these prefetches still consume slot attachments and KV cache warm-up GPU memory until eviction. Autoscaler reacts to transient drop in usable slots by attempting re-provisioning which amplifies allocation churn.
A: Churn causes prefetch re-execution -> confirmed by matching request ids and kv-cache misses
B: Autoscaler thrash increases fragmentation -> partially confirmed: autoscaler made 2 scale-down attempts in-window which coincided with additional eviction events
C: Underlying GPU IO errors (nvlink) are the root cause -> inconclusive; transient nvlink peer-drops observed but not clearly causal — further kernel-level logs requested from infra team
1) Temporary tenant throttling applied at edge to limit short-stream connect rate (reduced churn by ~60%) — immediate throughput improvement observed
2) Increased prefetch TTL to 2 minutes in the serving-runtime for this reservation to allow reuse across reconnects — reduced repeated warmups but increased short-lived memory hold times
3) Applied server-side keepalive guidance to customer SDK (recommended 30s) — pending customer rollout
4) Pinning the workload to a separate dedicated reservation as isolation short-term mitigation
Support (Asha): Asked customer for sample request ids, connection patterns, and traffic start/end timestamps.
Customer (AcmeChat - James Lee): Provided sample traffic trace and confirmed they launched a new client version yesterday that reduces connection pooling (likely cause).
SRE (Miguel): Collected serving-runtime heap profiles and scheduler allocation timeline; nvlink peer-drops seen but only during highest eviction windows. Attached metric snapshots to ticket.
Engineer (Priya Shah): Noted a known scheduler behavior where prefetch holds a slot attachment until KV warmup completes — suggested short-term TTL tuning and a medium-term scheduler change to avoid holding attachments for clients that disconnect quickly.
Support (Asha): Recommended customer enable client keepalive and provided SDK snippet; scheduled a call for 2026-03-11 to coordinate mitigation rollout.
1) SRE to gather kernel-level NVMe/NVLINK logs for gpux012 during the incident window (assigned to Miguel). 2) Engineering to prototype scheduler change that cancels prefetch attachments if client disconnects within X ms (PR sketch: runtime/prefetch-cancelation). 3) Customer to roll out client-side keepalive and connection pooling update; monitor p50/p99. 4) Consider short-term tenant isolation if churn persists.
In Progress - partial mitigations applied (tenant throttling and increased prefetch TTL). Awaiting customer SDK rollout and infra kernel logs to confirm or rule out hardware IO contribution. Follow-up actions: scheduler patch (PR linked), postmortem if repeats.
Add a dashboard tile showing prefetch_active_count alongside connects/min per tenant
Add autoscaler hysteresis for dedicated reservations experiencing high short-lived-connection churn
Implement runtime prefetch cancellation on client disconnect (engineering task)
Customer-facing best-practice doc for connection pooling and recommended keepalive settings

title: Initial byte delay observed during chat handshake after SSL negotiation and serving runtime update
body:
Initial byte delay observed during chat handshake after SSL negotiation and serving runtime update

Issue summary: Customers report elevated time-to-first-token (TTFB) for chat completions beginning immediately after a serving runtime update and concurrent SSL/TLS healthcheck change. Impact: Multiple enterprise customers (first report from HyperDocs Inc.) experienced 5–15s delays for the first token on new chat sessions; some requests hit client-side timeouts. Scope: observed across rw-3.5-chat and redwood-3b-quant variants in us-east-1.

Observed behavior: - New chat sessions show large gap between TCP/TLS handshake completion and the first byte emitted by upstream (server-side). - 95th percentile TTFB spiked from ~450ms to 6.2s starting at 2026-03-13T15:12Z. - No increase in token generation time once streaming begins.

Expected behavior: First token emitted within typical TTFB envelope (<1s p95) for pinned model/variant workloads.

1) Create new chat completion request to /v1/chat/completions with rw-3.5-chat pinned.
2) Ensure session has no warm cache (fresh client).
3) Measure time from request start to first streaming token.
4) Repeat across multiple workers (observed variability).

Notes: Reproduced reliably in prod us-east after the runtime rollout (2026-03-13 15:00Z) when TLS healthcheck flag was enabled.
Sample trace/channel: request_id=3f8a9b7c; LB: tcp_conn_established=2026-03-13T15:18:02.123Z; tls_handshake_complete=2026-03-13T15:18:02.245Z; upstream_first_byte=2026-03-13T15:18:08.512Z; ttfb=6.267s.
Edge LB logs show increased 'SYN_RECV' and a bump in 'conn_reuse=false' for affected flows.
Serving runtime span dump: wait_for_worker_pool 0.1s, acquire_connection 5.9s, send_request 0.02s, first_token_emit 0.005s.
Console dashboard: service/ttfb.p95 jumped to 6.2s; `model_warmup.time_to_ready` for new worker increased ~7s after rollout.

2026-03-13 15:25Z - SRE (Aisha Rahman): Correlated spike with runtime rollout and TLS healthcheck flag flip at 15:00Z. Load balancer shows many flows with no connection reuse.
Hypothesis A: TLS renegotiation / healthcheck change causing upstream connection re-creation and blocking worker warmup during first request.
Hypothesis B: Serving runtime connection pooling tweak introduced a blocking acquire path on cold connections (race between healthcheck and request path).
Evidence: Traces consistently show long time in 'acquire_connection' before any model work starts; once connection is established token emission is fast. No model compute regressions in profiler samples.
Reproduction in staging: Enabled the same TLS/healthcheck config in a staging cluster — p95 TTFB increased ~4.8s on cold sessions. Rolling back the healthcheck flag in staging returned p95 to baseline.
Temporary mitigation applied: Pinned HyperDocs traffic to previous runtime variant (runtime-v20260228) which restored normal TTFB for affected sessions.
Long-term action items: adjust connection pooling to avoid blocking on healthchecks, add a soft-warmup path to avoid synchronous acquire on first request, and add synthetic monitoring for handshake->first-byte latency.
Related telemetry: increased 504s for some long-running client SDKs due to client-side timeouts on first-token delays.
Next steps: Eng to reproduce and produce a minimal test harness for TLS+pooling interaction; schedule controlled rollout with canary for fixed runtime.

Workaround: Pinned affected customer traffic to previous runtime variant and adjusted LB routing to favor connection reuse. Root cause (provisional): interaction between new TLS/healthcheck behavior and serving runtime connection-pool acquire logic created a synchronous stall on cold upstream connections, delaying the first request by several seconds. Permanent fix planned: runtime patch to make connection acquire non-blocking with a soft-warmup path + LB healthcheck tuning. Postmortem and rollout plan to follow.

title: Tenant stuck on legacy model variant after rapid canary weight drift during traffic surge
body:
Tenant stuck on legacy model variant after rapid canary weight drift during traffic surge

Issue summary:
Customer (FinNova) reports that a subset of requests have been routed to an older model variant that they had explicitly pinned away from. The regression began during a customer traffic spike and a concurrent canary weight change.

Impact:
- ~18% of requests for one tenant are receiving outputs from the legacy variant (v1.8) instead of the intended pinned variant (v2.0-quant).
- Customer reports degraded result quality and elevated token usage leading to billing concerns.
- Problem started during a scheduled weighted canary adjustment and persisted despite control-plane restarts.

Environment:
- Redwood Dedicated pool (dedicated tenant pool, us-east region)
- Tenant: finnova-prod (dedicated)
- Affected model: redwood/oasst-7b-v2-quant (target), legacy fallback v1.8 (observed)
- Ingress path: edge-proxy -> orchestrator -> serving-runtime (quantized GPU nodes)

Steps to reproduce (from customer and support replay):
1) Customer increases concurrent sessions from ~1200 to ~3200 over 3 minutes (traffic surge window).
2) Support triggers canary weight shift from 5% -> 25% for v2.0-quant via Console rollout UI.
3) During the shift, certain sticky sessions begin receiving v1.8 responses; session affinity indicates a pin to legacy variant.
4) Attempts to refresh tenant pin via API return success but do not clear stuck affinity for affected sessions.

Observed behaviour:
- Sessions tied to a cohort continue to route to legacy variant even after pin-update and orchestration restart.
- Edge logs show the cohort affinity token is present, but orchestrator returns placement for legacy variant for that token.
- No 5xx errors; requests succeed but with unexpected variant.

Expected behaviour:
- Pin update should immediately route all new requests and existing sessions (subject to TTL) to pinned variant or trigger a clean handoff according to rollout policy.

Logs / Dashboards / Links:
- Support trace: https://console.redwood/support/traces/SUP-142357-rt-01
- Ingress sampling (edge-proxy): https://dash.redwood/edge/proxy/requests?trace=SUP-142357
- Orchestrator placement events: https://dash.redwood/orchestrator/events?range=3h
- Customer-provided transcript showing v1.8 outputs: attached as finnova_output_snippet.txt
- Related Slack thread: #support-finnova (slack.com/archives/C02XYZ/2026-03-12)

Initial hypothesis:
- During rapid weight change + surge, pin reconciliation logic failed to pick up the new placement snapshot and served an older placement for a subset of cohort tokens.
- Edge or sidecar cache may be returning stale affinity tokens that map to older cohort epoch.
- Orchestrator snapshot merge timing could create transient window where placement resolver prefers legacy nodes for tokens with intermediate epochs.

Impact assessment so far:
- Customer-facing but limited to a cohort (approx 18% of tenant traffic).
- No increased error rates or node OOMs; primarily correctness / quality and billing exposure.

Immediate mitigation attempted:
- Force pin-refresh for finnova via admin API (admin.routing.refresh_pins(tenant=finnova-prod)) — reported success but did not clear affected live sessions.
- Rolling restart of orchestrator worker behind tenant shard performed at 2026-03-12 15:40 UTC — did not rectify stuck cohort.
- Temporary rule applied on edge to reject affinity cookies older than epoch-245 to force rebind (edge config change ID: edgecfg-2026-03-12-1346). Observed 70% of stuck sessions rebind within 6 minutes, remaining ~30% persisted.

Next steps (in progress):
- SRE to instrument placement resolver trace for token->epoch mapping (assigned).
- Routing team to review snapshot merge logic and any prefetch/caching decisions during weight changes.
- Run targeted session reshard job to clear remaining stuck cohort (requires scheduled maintenance window with customer).
- Engineering to prepare a hotfix to make pin-refresh force-evict session affinity when requested by admin API.

Reproduced in staging by simulating 3-minute ramp from 1.2k -> 3.2k concurrent sessions and applying a 5%->25% canary weight shift. Traced token->placement mapping; found ~27% of tokens referenced stale epoch (one snapshot behind). Orchestrator logs show snapshot merge fences executing but a race condition in the token resolver allowed lookups against an older snapshot until its TTL expired. title: Intermittent multiplexed SSE session stall when mobile app is backgrounded, partial final output on reconnect
body:
Intermittent multiplexed SSE session stall when mobile app is backgrounded, partial final output on reconnect

Issue summary: Customer reports that when their iOS app (WKWebView-backed) is backgrounded and later resumed, SSE streams that were multiplexed over a single connection frequently stall and deliver only a partial final token/metadata bundle on reconnect. Impact: end users see truncated assistant replies or replies missing the final choice metadata (finish_reason, token_offsets). This affects conversational flows and causes retries in their client that double-bill tokens in some cases. Environment: prod us-east, multiplexed sessions enabled, client SDK v1.8.2.
Roughly 7-12% of streaming sessions from this customer across us-east show truncated final output after background/resume. Several paid users reported missing final paragraphs; affects live chat UX and billing correctness.
1) Start a streaming chat request using multiplexed SSE (client creates a single SSE connection with multiple client-id headers).
2) Allow the assistant to stream a multi-paragraph response (~350-800 tokens).
3) Background the iOS app (home button / swipe up) before the stream completes and leave for 20-40s.
4) Resume the app and let the client re-establish the multiplexed connection and issue a resume/reconnect for the in-flight client-id.
5) Observe that the resumed session sometimes receives a partial final fragment or never receives terminal metadata (finish_reason) while the server shows request complete in logs.
On reconnect the client receives earlier chunks but final chunk either never arrives or arrives without terminal metadata. Server logs show the request completed and tokens emitted, but the multiplexed session control frames are not consistently delivered to the resumed stream. Client-side retries trigger duplicate billing in ~3% of affected cases.
After background/resume and reconnect, the resumed multiplexed session should receive all remaining chunks including final token(s) and terminal metadata exactly once, with SDK-level de-duplication preventing double billing.
Sample server trace: request_id=req-0a5c3b; timeline: accepted->streaming->complete (token_count=512). SSE connection id=conn-8f12 shows heartbeat gap at T+22s. Proxy logs (nginx) show client FIN then SYN re-open with same session-id but missing last 1 KB of buffered frames. Client SDK debug: resume_ack received but terminal 'end' control frame not observed. Attached excerpts available in support portal (link withheld).
Advise customer to disable multiplexing on mobile SDK for affected release (per-client SSE connection) and enable client-side buffer/retry with idempotency token to avoid duplicate billing. They reported this reduced occurrence to <0.5% in a canary.

Proposed patch to serving-runtime and a smaller proxy config change to extend short buffer eviction window.

Mitigation in progress: proxy canary deployed in us-east; customer instructed to disable multiplexing as short-term workaround. Full fix requires serving-runtime patch; targeted rollout planned. Ticket will be updated when patch is in production and customer confirms resolution.

title: Prospect question: were caching and/or batching enabled in published latency/$ benchmark numbers?
body:
Prospect question: were caching and/or batching enabled in published latency/$ benchmark numbers?

Issue summary:
Prospect (Summit Legaltech) reviewing the public benchmark report asked whether the published latency/$ numbers were achieved with caching and/or batching enabled, and specifically whether results benefited from cross-request prompt caching.

Customer question (verbatim excerpt):
"Are the latency/$ numbers assuming caching or batching? If you had prefix/prompt caching turned on, that could skew results depending on prompt overlap. We need to understand what was enabled by default vs configured." 

Context:
- Inquiry came in after Sales shared the report link during early evaluation.
- They are comparing the report to internal PoC assumptions and want clarity on what’s “real-world” vs “best-case.”

Impact:
- Sales cycle risk if methodology is perceived as cherry-picked.
- Needs a crisp, repeatable answer + linkable source.

Requested outcome:
1) Confirm whether continuous batching was enabled.
2) Confirm whether cross-request caching (prompt/prefix/KV reuse across requests) was enabled.
3) Point to the canonical methodology section with the caching/batching policy and caveats.

Notes:
- Keep wording aligned with Legal guidelines: describe settings plainly; avoid claims like “identical to every customer workload.”
- Provide suggested phrasing for AE/SE to reuse.
2025-07-10 09:18 PT — Jasmine Liu (Reporter): Logging this as a Q from Summit Legaltech (prospect). They’re concerned our benchmark may be advantaged by caching. Requesting a canonical answer and the right methodology link to send.
2025-07-10 10:02 PT — Renee Sullivan (Assignee): I’ll draft response + pull exact wording from the methodology doc. Flagging Jonas/Claire for confirmation on the caching/batching policy used in the sweeps.
2025-07-10 10:26 PT — Renee Sullivan: @Jonas Weber / @Claire Dubois — can you confirm what was enabled for the public runs? Specifically: (a) continuous batching, (b) cross-request prompt/prefix caching, (c) any special cache warming beyond standard warmup iterations. Need a 2–3 sentence customer-safe explanation.
2025-07-10 11:11 PT — Jonas Weber: For the published sweeps we ran with production serving behavior (continuous batching enabled) but did NOT use cross-request prompt/prefix caching. Prompt sets are intentionally low-overlap to avoid cache effects. We did standard warmup to stabilize kernels/allocations before measuring. Within-request KV cache is always used (that’s fundamental to transformer decoding, not a ‘benchmark trick’).
2025-07-10 11:24 PT — Claire Dubois: +1. Add nuance: we did not enable any response caching or application-layer caching. Batching was constrained by latency SLO targets (not max-throughput mode). We also publish p50/p95 and rerun when variance exceeds threshold (stability gates).
2025-07-10 12:05 PT — Renee Sullivan: Drafting external reply now. Will link to the public methodology section and clarify: continuous batching ON, cross-request prompt/prefix caching OFF, no response caching, standard warmup only; prompt set designed to minimize overlap; results represent a defined workload profile (prefill/decode mix), not every workload.
2025-07-10 12:47 PT — Renee Sullivan (to customer, via email): Sent response + link to methodology. Included a short paragraph AE can reuse. Also offered a quick 15-min call to map their workload (long context / RAG) to the closest benchmark slice and discuss how caching would change their unit economics.
2025-07-11 08:36 PT — Jasmine Liu: Customer acknowledged and said this addresses their main concern. They want a follow-up on how to reproduce numbers for their prompts; routing to Markus/SE separately.
Provided canonical explanation and source link:
- Continuous batching: enabled (production serving behavior), tuned for the benchmark’s latency targets rather than max-throughput mode.
- Cross-request caching (prompt/prefix reuse across requests): not enabled for published runs.
- Response/application caching: not used.
- Warmup: standard warmup iterations performed prior to measurement to avoid cold-start artifacts.
- Within-request KV cache: used as part of normal transformer decoding (not a special benchmark optimization).

Shared methodology link and offered guidance for reproducing results with their prompt distribution.
Thanks for the question — we wanted to make sure the benchmark reflects production serving behavior without relying on workload-specific cache advantages.

For the published runs:
- Continuous batching was enabled (as it is in normal production serving), and configured to meet the benchmark’s latency targets rather than “max throughput at any cost.”
- Cross-request prompt/prefix caching (reusing KV/prefixes across separate requests) was *not* enabled for the published numbers, and the prompt set is designed to minimize overlap so results aren’t dominated by cache hit rate.
- We did not use response/application-layer caching.

Full details (workload definition, warmup, stability/variance gates, and metric definitions) are in the methodology section here: <public methodology link>.
If pushed on ‘is batching a benchmark trick?’: position batching as an industry-standard production technique; clarify we’re not measuring single-request isolated latency, but a defined concurrency + workload mix that mirrors common production conditions. Avoid implying results match every customer configuration; point to reproducibility harness/Docker runner if they request PoC replication steps.
No further action required for Support. If Summit wants replication guidance, coordinate with Markus Klein (Solutions) and point them to the reproducibility notes + recommended PoC plan (workload-matched prompts, fixed model version, fixed region, repeated runs with stability thresholds).

title: Rate-limit skew and repeated 429s after subaccount transfer during bulk embedding import
body:
Rate-limit skew and repeated 429s after subaccount transfer during bulk embedding import

Issue summary: Customer reports persistent 429 responses when performing a large embeddings import immediately after transferring 5 subaccounts under a single organization billing pool. Impact: Import jobs failing with repeated 429s causing incomplete ingestion and downstream blocking of model-indexing pipelines. Environment: Dedicated tenancy on prod-us-east, dedicated pool id dp-42. Recent customer action: executed subaccount transfer and billing consolidation at 02:00 UTC before starting import.

Observed behavior: Multiple workers (50 parallel processes) receive 429s within 10-30s of start; headers show per-key token refill lag and inconsistent X-RateLimit-* headers across parallel requests. Console shows quota for the top-level org updated, but subaccount windows appear to have stale refill counters. Customer sees repeated retries with exponential backoff and still exhausts the window. Expected behavior: Post-transfer quota and refill windows should reconcile quickly and allow sustained throughput given dedicated commit.

Customer impact: High — scheduled migration/import must complete for production search indexing. Customer has deadline for compliance decommissioning and indicated potential business impact if import cannot finish within SLA.
1) Create organization with 5 subaccounts under a single billing pool. 2) Move the 5 subaccounts from separate billing pools into the target pool (simulate transfer). 3) Immediately start bulk embeddings import with 50 parallel workers using the existing API keys for the subaccounts. 4) Observe HTTP 429 responses within the first minute and inconsistent X-RateLimit headers returned. 5) Repeat with smaller concurrency to validate behavior changes.
- Sample response headers captured 2026-03-11T02:15:23Z: HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests; X-RateLimit-Limit: 6000; X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0; X-RateLimit-Reset: 167; Retry-After: 8
- API gateway logs show token_debit failures tied to org_id=arcadia-876 and subaccount ids s-101,s-102,s-103.
- Console audit: billing_pool update event id bp-20260311-09, completed at 02:01:12Z.
- Worker client stack traces show retry loop attempts and backoff jitter up to 64s.

- Hypothesis 1: Refill window for per-subaccount token buckets was not atomically migrated leading to uneven starting credits.
- Hypothesis 2: Rate-limiter shard responsible for these subaccounts did not observe the billing-pool reconciliation event and is using stale refill state.
- Hypothesis 3: Dedicated pool tiering logic applied a short warmup (burst-limited) window after the transfer which is blocking sustained concurrency.
- Early checks: Confirmed billing event present in audit logs. Token bucket metrics show high debit rate and zeroed remaining counters immediately after transfer.
- Checked gateway traces: transfer event propagated to control-plane but rate-limiter shard commit timestamps lag by ~30s.
- Reproduced in staging with smaller scale: when transfer is followed immediately by parallel imports, 429s are observed until ~45s after transfer completion.

Priya Nair (Support): Collected headers and gateway traces from customer. Asked for exact start time and worker concurrency — customer provided timings and sample tokens.
Marco Silva (SRE): Noted potential race in quota reconciliation. Will pull shard commit logs and check for missing publish ack from billing service.
SRE Team (internal): Found control-plane publish to 'quota-reconciler' succeeded but deliver to rate-limiter-kv-store delayed by 28s. Possible queue consumer lag on rl-sync worker.
Support (to customer): Suggested two immediate mitigations — staggered worker start (ramp up over 60s) or run import against a single API key tied to the org-level pool (avoid per-subaccount windows) until we confirm fix.
Workaround provided: customer accepted a staged ramp-up script and switched to a single org-level API key for the import; import completed with reduced failures. Engineering action: Opened internal task to harden quota-reconciler -> rate-limiter delivery with guaranteed-at-least-once semantics and backfill reconciliation for subaccount counters. Proposed fix: add a short 'post-transfer grace window' where org-level tokens are used until all shards confirm updated state. Related PR opened: github.com/redwood-inference/rate-limiter/pull/342. Follow-up: schedule change to rate-limiter consumer to reduce lag and add observability alerts for reconciliation deltas. Customer to re-test a replica transfer next week and coordinate with SRE during the window.
1) SRE to add consumer lag metric and alert (ETA 2026-03-14). 2) Eng to implement grace-window fallback and add unit/integration tests (tracked in internal ticket INT-22018). 3) Support to coordinate a controlled re-test with Arcadia Health and monitor metrics in real-time. 4) Document recommended post-transfer importing pattern in KB article.

title: Okta group name encoding mismatch in identity-proxy prevents console & DB admin role resolution
body:
Okta group name encoding mismatch in identity-proxy prevents console & DB admin role resolution

Issue summary:
Several internal engineers (DB admins + SREs) were unable to access the internal Console and the Grafana DB-admin dashboard after a routine Okta group membership sync. Users were authenticated by Okta but authorization failed because RBAC role resolution did not find expected group claims in the token assertion.

Impact:
- ~12 engineers reported 403 on Console and Grafana when trying to access DB admin or infra dashboards.
- Deploys requiring DB-admin approvals were delayed ~90 minutes for one team.
- No production-serving traffic impacted (hosts/app endpoints healthy).

Environment:
- Prod identity flow via Okta OIDC -> identity-proxy -> console (us-east cluster).
- Affected roles: grafana:db-admin, console:infra-admin.

Initial hypothesis:
- Group claim mapping was missing or Okta SCIM sync failed.
- RBAC rules might have changed during a recent role cleanup.

Observations / why this is unusual:
- Okta auth logs show successful assertion with group claim present.
- identity-proxy request logs show group claim arriving, but the value seen by the console service is different (percent-encoded vs plus-encoded).
- Affected Okta groups contain a literal plus sign in the name (e.g., "db-admin+prod", "infra-team+east"). This is uncommon and was introduced by a naming convention change three weeks ago.
1) Authenticate via Okta SSO with a user who belongs to a group containing a '+' in the name (example user: emma.stone@redwood.com).
2) Follow OIDC redirect to identity-proxy.
3) Observe token forwarded to console service; check /v1/token/introspect or identity-proxy debug header 'x-forwarded-groups'.
4) Compare Okta assertion group claim to what console receives (difference in encoding).
5) Attempt to access a DB-admin-restricted path, receive 403.
- Okta system log (event id okta-20260310-778): group claim contains 'db-admin+prod'.
- identity-proxy access log: forwarded_groups=['db-admin%2Bprod'] on request id ip-req-5a3b.
- console auth debug: received_groups header shows 'db-admin%252Bprod' (double-encoded).
- Grafana policy engine audit: no match for 'db-admin%252Bprod' against role mapping 'db-admin+prod' -> 403.
- Relevant commit: identity-proxy@master 7f9b3e2 (URL-decode normalization added, merged 2026-03-09).
- Screenshots and request traces attached in the ticket (links to internal S3).
- Reproduced locally by creating an Okta test group 'db-admin+prod' and performing OIDC flow: identity-proxy now decodes URL-encoded groups then accidentally runs a second decode path in header serialization, resulting in percent-encoded string being passed through twice (percent sign becomes %25).
- Root cause narrowed to identity-proxy middleware introduced in PR 4123: normalization RFC attempted to 'normalize' incoming claims by running url.QueryUnescape unconditionally and then encoding for header safety; the header encoding path expects raw '+' semantics and ends up double-encoding a literal '+'.
- Historical note: previous flows treated '+' as literal character; change was intended to handle spaces encoded as '+', but Okta emits '+' for literal plus in group names, which the normalization code doesn't distinguish.
- No Okta release or SCIM change at time of incident; this is an identity-proxy regression.
- Linked edge case: some downstream services perform a single decode before RBAC matching; others do not, causing inconsistent behavior across services.

Temporary mitigations tried:
- Reverting the normalization in a staging instance reproduced expected behavior.
- Patch applied locally to identity-proxy container to skip double-decode for group claim header; this restored access for test users.
- Added a short-lived admission rule to console service to apply decode-normalization as a stopgap, but it's not safe for all downstreams.

Impact assessment:
- Incident scope limited to identities with '+' in group name (~0.8% of groups). Most users unaffected.
- Elevated business risk because those groups map to high-privilege roles.
Workaround applied: rolled back identity-proxy commit 7f9b3e2 (normalization) in prod at 2026-03-11 02:00 UTC which restored expected group semantics.
Permanent fix: landed identity-proxy PR 4130 that implements claim normalization with explicit rules: detect '+' as literal when Okta group claim contains '+' and avoid QueryUnescape for that header; added unit tests and end-to-end test with Okta emulator.
Rollout plan:
- 2026-03-12 09:00 UTC: Canary deploy PR 4130 to 10% identity-proxy instances in us-east (passed smoke tests).
- 2026-03-12 11:15 UTC: Gradual rollout to remaining prod instances with health checks.
Follow-ups:
- Add a lint check in onboarding to warn about special characters in Okta group names.
- Update Confluence runbook 'Okta Claim Normalization' with decoding rules and test vectors.
- Postmortem scheduled with SRE and Identity team on 2026-03-15.
Add unit & integration tests for group-name edge cases (+, space, % encoding) in identity-proxy
Review Okta group naming policy and add warning in onboarding docs
Add monitoring alert to detect spike in 403 for admin roles (rule: 403_count for console-admin paths > 5 in 10m)
Run tabletop postmortem and publish findings to Confluence (due 2026-03-18)

title: Alt-Svc header inserted by corporate TLS-inspection proxy causes gRPC/HTTP2 stream fan-out and long-tail streaming latency
body:
Alt-Svc header inserted by corporate TLS-inspection proxy causes gRPC/HTTP2 stream fan-out and long-tail streaming latency

Issue summary:
Customer reports intermittent high tail latency (>5s) and duplicate frames during streaming chat responses from a Private deployment. The customer is on an enterprise private deployment behind a corporate TLS inspection appliance.

Impact:
- 25% of streaming sessions experience long-tail stalls or duplicated fragments leading to truncated messages.
- Customer-facing app shows degraded UX (stalls, partial transcripts).
- No model compute errors; request succeeds eventually or falls back to non-streaming response which increases token cost.

Environment:
- Private deployment in customer VPC (us-east-1) with VPC egress through corp security stack (TLS-inspecting proxy + outbound web gateway).
- Redwood Private agent version: 2026.02.3
- Serving runtime: 1.14.7

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) From inside customer network, open a streaming chat session via the Redwood client pinned to customer-pinned:gpt-3.5-finovate-v1.
2) Observe initial streaming tokens; after ~2-10s some sessions either: a) stall for 3-10s then resume with duplicate fragments, or b) produce a short truncated stream and the SDK retries producing a second stream.
3) Reproduced on multiple clients and via curl + http2 request to the customer-private endpoint.

Relevant logs / traces:
- Agent-side tcpdump (provided): repeated TCP connections with server-initiated RST after HTTP/2 SETTINGS exchange on sessions that later exhibit stalls.
- App-level trace: HTTP/2 stream resets (RST_STREAM) with code NO_ERROR; repeated connection re-negotiation.
- Edge proxy logs: evidence of Alt-Svc header being injected on 443 responses pointing to an internal proxy host (altproxy.corp:443).
- TLS cert chain on affected sessions shows interception cert (corp intermediate) — customer confirms HTTPS inspection is in-line.

Initial hypothesis:
- Corporate TLS inspection appliance is injecting Alt-Svc responses (or rewriting response metadata) which actively signals clients to attempt alternate endpoints. The Redwood client / SDK then opens additional HTTP/2/HTTP3 attempts or rebinds ALPN preferences, causing stream duplication and connection churn. Intermittent RST/NO_ERROR indicates graceful connection termination on the client side rather than server crash.

Why this is customer-impacting for Private deployments:
- Private agents rely on consistent ALPN/NPN negotiation and SNI behavior; middlebox-induced Alt-Svc/Alt-Authority changes can lead clients to open parallel transports or prematurely close streams. This behavior is more common when corporate appliances perform application-layer header synthesis for performance filtering or traffic steering.

Asked from customer:
- Full packet capture (pcap) and proxy logs (provided)
- List of internal proxy rules and whether Alt-Svc/Alt-Authority rewrite is enabled (pending)

2026-03-12 13:18 - Raj Patel: Acknowledged. Requested sample curl + --http2-v2 output and edge logs. Assigned to me for initial triage.

2026-03-13 09:22 - Customer (Finovate Cloud Services): Confirmed they can toggle a rule; will test disabling Alt-Svc injection later today and report back.
2026-03-13 19:55 - Raj Patel: Added mitigation guidance to customer. Also opened INT-9128 to prototype an SDK flag to ignore Alt-Svc hints when using pinned private endpoints.
2026-03-14 07:30 - Customer: After disabling Alt-Svc injection, long-tail stalls dropped to <1% in our canary tests across 200 streams.
Confirmed Alt-Svc header present on affected responses: Server was not adding this header but the corp proxy was synthesizing 'Alt-Svc: h3="altproxy.corp:443"; ma=2592000' on 200 responses.
Client/SDK behavior: When Alt-Svc points to an internal host, libhttp2/libcurl attempts alternative transports and may pipeline attempts; our streaming reconnection logic opens a new stream on connection change which leads to duplicate fragments.
Packet-level finding: pcap shows complete TLS handshake with inspection cert then HTTP/2 SETTINGS -> DATA -> RST_STREAM. The timing matches the client's reaction to Alt-Svc hints.
Risk assessment: High for enterprise private deployments where inspection appliances actively perform response rewriting. Not a general platform bug but an interoperability edge-case causing degraded UX and extra downstream load.
Workaround evaluated: Disabling Alt-Svc injection at the corporate proxy eliminates the symptom. Temporary SDK/config mitigation (ignore-alt-svc-for-private=true) reduces risk of fan-out but needs careful testing across HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 fallback paths.
Mitigation applied: Customer disabled Alt-Svc header synthesis at the corporate TLS inspection appliance — immediate improvement confirmed in canary tests. Follow-ups: (1) Ship SDK option to ignore Alt-Svc hints for pinned private endpoints (INT-9128) to avoid reliance on customer proxy configuration, PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/inference-runtime/pull/2981. (2) Update Private deployment runbook to call out Alt-Svc/Alt-Authority header synthesis as a known incompatibility and include recommended proxy rule examples. (3) Advise customers to whitelist Redwood endpoints or disable Alt-Svc/Alt-Authority rewriting for egress paths to avoid stream fan-out.

2) Docs: Update runbook + KB article with troubleshooting steps and packet examples (owner: Developer Experience).
3) Customer follow-up: Confirm 48-hour stability window and then move ticket to Resolved if no regressions (owner: Emma Chen).

title: Unexpected 429s during GraphQL multiplexing tenant cutover causing per-key misattribution
body:
Unexpected 429s during GraphQL multiplexing tenant cutover causing per-key misattribution

Issue summary: Customer reported sustained 429 responses for a subset of GraphQL mutation requests during a tenant cutover that started at ~2026-03-10T02:15Z. The traffic pattern was primarily background orchestration + user-facing GraphQL batching over long-lived HTTP/2 connections. Impact: Intermittent 429s for ~30% of requests from multiple API keys belonging to the migrating tenant; user-facing errors and delayed background jobs. Environment: Dedicated deployment (dedicated pool id d-44f2), prod, primary ingress in us-east-1 with geo-failover to eu-west-1. Steps to reproduce: 1) Customer did rolling migration of subaccount from old-tenant -> new-tenant using orchestrator that rotates API keys in-place while maintaining keepalive connections. 2) Multiple API keys reused over single multiplexed HTTP/2 connection via GraphQL batcher. 3) During cutover, we observed mixed attribution of tokens on the same connection. 4) Resulting rate-accounting counted some requests against the old tenant and some against the new tenant depending on in-flight header rewrite timing, leading to transient quota exhaustion and 429s. Relevant logs/snippets: - ingress log excerpt: "rate_limit_exceeded tenant=old-tn-73 key=ak_old_XXX window_id=2026-03-10T02:16Z conn_id=conn-7f3b path=/graphql batch_id=842" - batcher trace: "batch[842] keys=[ak_old_XXX, ak_new_YYY] multiplexed_by=graphql-batcher-1" - rate-limiter metric: "token_consumed_count spike at 02:15:20 correlates with key-rotation events" Additional notes: Customer uses per-route priority weighting and had recently enabled default connection affinity=keepalive-global. They reported the problem started immediately after cutover orchestration.
2026-03-10 03:04 - Support (Maya Chen): Acknowledged ticket, requested full ingress logs and the orchestrator timeline from the customer. Asked if cutover used simultaneous key rotation or sequential swap.
2026-03-10 04:10 - Customer (Carlos M. @ CartaHealth): Provided orchestrator logs. Keys are rotated using a zero-downtime strategy that rebinds env vars while reusing existing TCP/HTTP/2 connections for speed.
2026-03-10 08:30 - Support (Maya Chen): Reproduced a small test in staging by replaying rotation while reusing HTTP/2 connections; observed mixed attribution in rate-logs. Escalated to SRE/Ingress team and created INT-3321.
2026-03-11 11:22 - SRE (Oliver Grant): Confirmed race between header rewrite and per-connection token attribution in the ingress proxy. Noted that our current model attributes quota by connection for performance; when multiple keys are presented on a single connection we fall back to last-seen attribution which can flip mid-batch.
2026-03-12 16:45 - Eng (Priya Rao): Draft fix: change attribution to per-request header read (cost: small latency increase) and add connection drain on key rotation. Opened PR to ingress: https://github.com/redwood-inference/ingress/pull/981. Deployed hotfix binary to eu-west-1 staging for validation.
2026-03-13 09:10 - Support (Maya Chen): Applied customer-facing mitigation: asked customer to temporarily enable connection_affinity: per_key on their dedicated route and to perform key rotation in sequential drain mode. Customer implemented the change and reported immediate reduction in 429s.
2026-03-13 14:05 - Customer (Carlos M. @ CartaHealth): Confirmed service recovered to baseline; no more 429s observed during subsequent rotations. Asked for guidance on permanent configuration and whether global keepalive can be kept.
2026-03-13 15:30 - Eng (Oliver Grant): Noted PR merged to master; rollout scheduled to us-east-1 on 2026-03-14. Followup action: add explicit warning in docs when using key-rotation + keepalive-global and add an automated drain helper in the orchestrator templates.
Observed correlation between key-rotation events in customer's orchestrator and spikes in token_consumed_count in ingress rate-limiter graphs.
Root cause: ingress attributed quota on a per-connection basis (performance optimization). Reusing a connection across multiple API keys during a migration allows mid-flight attribution flips and double-counting against different tenant token buckets.
Repro in staging: replayed orchestrator sequence with HTTP/2 multiplexing; identical 429 footprint when affinity=keepalive-global. With connection_affinity=per_key the problem disappears.
Edge case: GraphQL batcher groups requests from multiple api-keys into a single downstream batch; this amplifies misattribution because a single batch can contain requests intended for different tenants.
Mitigation validated: connection_affinity: per_key + sequential key rotation + short connection drain period (30s) prevents mixed attribution.
Long-term fix: switch to per-request header attribution and add explicit connection drain on key rotation in ingress proxy (PR #981).
Workaround applied and validated with customer: set connection_affinity to per_key on the affected route and perform sequential key rotation with a 30s connection drain window. Engineering merged a fix to attribute quota per-request (PR 981) and scheduled rollout to us-east-1 on 2026-03-14; post-rollout, we expect the issue to be fully mitigated even with keepalive-global. Follow-up actions: update runbook and add an orchestrator template that performs drain+rotate, communicate guidance to dedicated customers performing key rotations.
Add runbook section: 'Safe API key rotation on dedicated pools' with exact config flags and drain timings.
Instrument ingress metric export to include per-connection key-set snapshot during rotation windows to simplify future debugging.
Notify Customer Success to reach out and confirm stable behavior after full us-east-1 rollout.
Consider adding server-side rate-limit header that shows which tenant/bucket a request was counted against to help customers triage in real time.

title: Finalized invoice contains negative usage line and missing promo credit after mid-cycle coupon reversal
body:
Finalized invoice contains negative usage line and missing promo credit after mid-cycle coupon reversal

Issue summary:
Customer was issued a mid-cycle coupon reversal (promo code REACT-30) on 2026-03-11. Invoice for billing period 2026-03-01 to 2026-03-12 finalized on 2026-03-12 and shows: a negative usage line (-1,234 tokens, treated as refund) labelled 'promo-reversal-adjustment' and no corresponding coupon credit line. Customer expects the canceled coupon to produce a single negative credit adjustment, not a phantom usage line; net owed should have been unchanged after reversal.

Impact:
- Customer BrightMap Analytics reports their finalized invoice shows an unexpected negative usage line and is short the expected promo credit. They are concerned about accounting and tax reporting.

Timeline / Background:
- 2026-03-10: Promo REACT-30 applied to account for a trial campaign.
- 2026-03-11 08:22 UTC: Customer requested cancellation of promo; support issued coupon reversal request.
- 2026-03-11 08:23 UTC: Billing service enqueued coupon-reversal postback.
- 2026-03-12 02:00 UTC: Hourly metering run and invoice finalization job executed for customer.
- 2026-03-12 02:05 UTC: Delayed postback processed by reconciler, created a negative usage adjustment record, and did not attach an invoice credit line.

Steps to reproduce (internal):
1) Identify customer org ID (provided separately).
2) Re-run invoice finalization for 2026-03-12 in staging with replayed postbacks with original timing (simulate delayed postback after finalization).
3) Observe line items produced by invoice-compiler service and compare to expected credit memo flow.

Observed behavior:
- Invoice-compiler produced a negative usage line item labeled 'promo-reversal-adjustment' with delta -$12.34 and no separate 'promo credit' invoice line.
- Finance dashboard shows mismatch between postback audit and invoice ledger.

Expected behavior:
- Coupon reversal should create either a single credit memo line associated to the invoice or be deferred to the next invoice depending on the reversal timestamp, but not create a phantom negative usage line on a finalized invoice without an accompanying credit memo.

Logs / evidence:
- Billing reconciler log excerpts (2026-03-12 02:04:57 UTC): "Processed reversal postback for promo REACT-30; marking adjustment type=credit_memo if invoice_open else queue_next; final action=usage_adjustment"

title: Guidance requested: split refill windows for background telemetry pulses vs interactive realtime streams
body:
Guidance requested: split refill windows for background telemetry pulses vs interactive realtime streams

Customer runs a mixed workload in production: interactive realtime chat sessions (low tokens, high concurrency) and frequent background telemetry/heartbeat pings from a fleet of edge agents. Over the last week they started seeing a rising number of 429s that correlate with telemetry sweep windows. They want concrete guidance on whether to: 1) split refill windows (separate burst pools) for telemetry vs interactive lanes, 2) use separate API keys/routes for telemetry, or 3) tune smoothing/refill intervals to avoid synchronized tenant-level throttles.
~12% of interactive chat requests returned 429s during nightly telemetry sweeps; several customer-facing flows degrade (timeouts, retries). Affects production us-west region only. Billing unaffected but user experience degraded.
1) Deploy 1000 edge agents configured to send telemetry heartbeat (small POST) every 60 seconds. 2) Start 200 concurrent interactive chat sessions that send occasional messages (avg 30 tokens) over WebSocket/HTTP3. 3) Observe token usage and 429 spikes in request timeline around minute boundaries when many heartbeats align. 4) Toggle telemetry heartbeat jitter and re-run to see effect.
Sample throttle header from client: X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0, X-RateLimit-Reset: 25s. Platform logs show tenant_token_window_exhausted events at 2026-03-09T03:00:00Z and 2026-03-10T03:00:00Z. Ingress traces show many short lived HTTP/3 connections from telemetry agents and long-lived websocket-like streams for chat. No 5xx accompanying errors.
Initial hypothesis: telemetry heartbeats are concentrated on the same refill epoch and are counted against the tenant-wide refill window used by interactive requests. HTTP/3 multipath and short connections may be causing preflight-like counting or connection-level aggregation anomalies. Possible contributing factors: (a) telemetry uses same API key/route and is not isolated, (b) refill interval (60s epoch) aligns with heartbeat cadence resulting in sawtooth token consumption, (c) smoothing parameters not tuned for high-cardinality short requests.
1) Recommend separating telemetry onto a dedicated API key and route that maps to a distinct burst pool (isolated burst lane) so background pings cannot exhaust interactive quota. 2) If separate key not possible, add jitter to heartbeat schedule to desynchronize pulses. 3) Temporarily increase tenant burst credits during sweep windows or configure a short-lived exception for telemetry route via Console as a stopgap.
Triage stage. Guidance prepared for customer; engineering inboxed to evaluate adding a Console UI path to create isolated burst pools for routes. If customer agrees, support will schedule a config change: create dedicated route + API key for telemetry and update docs with recommended jitter parameters. No code changes required immediately.

title: Persistent 5xx pulses during tenant concurrency surge caused by runtime file descriptor exhaustion
body:
Persistent 5xx pulses during tenant concurrency surge caused by runtime file descriptor exhaustion

Issue summary: Customer reported repeated short-lived waves of 5xx (502/503) affecting streaming and short-poll generation routes for a single dedicated tenant. Impact: Several production endpoints returned 502/503 intermittently for ~10-30s pulses, causing dropped streams and failed request retries; observed by Nimbus Health as increased error rate and user-visible failures. Environment: Dedicated pool for customer in us-east-1; mixed embedding/chat traffic; model pinned to redwood/gptx-3.2. Initial symptom window: 2026-03-10 01:12–03:40 UTC.

Steps to reproduce: not reliably reproducible from a single synthetic test; reproduces under sustained concurrent tenant traffic + aggressive background prefetch for large prompt sets. Support template fields below contain logs, metrics, and timeline.
Send mixed streaming and non-streaming requests at 150 concurrent connections from single tenant with varied prompt lengths (200–400 tokens).
Trigger background model prefetch by submitting a large-batch evaluation job (customer internal test) to the tenant simultaneously.
Observe intermittent 502/503 on streaming sessions and short-lived elevated 5xx pulses in API gateway and runtime metrics.
2026-03-10T01:15:04Z runtime[pid=1843]: OSError: [Errno 24] Too many open files
2026-03-10T01:15:04Z runtime[pid=1843]: Traceback (most recent call last): File "/opt/serving/prefetch/worker.py", line 412, in _open_prefetch_stream

API gateway 5xx rate for tenant spiked from baseline 0.2% to 8.6% in 30s windows

Accept queue drop rate increased concurrently with runtime 'watchdog restart' events

Initial triage (support): Correlated apigw 502s to upstream runtime restarts and EMFILE in runtime logs. Tenant traffic patterns show high short-lived stream connects plus a background evaluation triggering prefetch activity.
SRE ran live diagnostics on affected runtime host: lsof snapshot showed thousands of TCP sockets and many /tmp/prefetch/*.tmp file handles left open by prefetch worker processes.
Hypothesis: Prefetch worker has a filehandle leak when prefetching large prompt embeddings; under high concurrency the leak climbs until process cannot open sockets/files, watchdog restarts the worker and upstream returns 502/503.
Temporary mitigation: increased ulimit -n for affected pods to 100k and disabled aggressive prefetch for the tenant via per-tenant config (rollback to conservative prefetch window). This immediately reduced recurrence of pulses.
Root cause identified by runtime eng: missing close() paths in prefetch worker error-handling when partial reads fail; also prefetch created temp files that were not removed on cancellation. See PRs referenced.
